title: The Cell Bench
summary: Find terminal voltage, internal resistance and charging current, and combine cells in series and parallel.
subject: physics
concepts: Charging a battery, V = ε + Ir
Cells in series and in parallel
learningOutcome: The student can find the current and terminal voltage of a real cell, measure its internal resistance, analyse charging, and combine cells in series and in parallel.

levels.title: A real cell
levels.adds: Baseline: I = ε/(R + r) and V = ε − Ir, the terminal voltage is less than the emf (Ex 3.2).
hints: The cell's internal resistance is in series with the resistor.
Current is the emf divided by the total resistance.
The terminal voltage is the emf minus the voltage lost inside, Ir.

levels.title: Hidden resistance
levels.adds: New idea: measure r from a reading, r = (ε − V)/I, and the short-circuit current is ε/r (Ex 3.1).
hints: Slide the load and read both meters.
The voltage missing from the emf is the volts lost inside the cell.
The largest current flows when the load resistance is zero.

levels.title: Charging a battery
levels.adds: New idea: while charging V = ε + Ir, and a series resistor limits the current (Ex 3.8).
hints: The supply and the battery's emf oppose, so I = (V − ε)/(R + r).
The current now enters the positive terminal, so the terminal voltage exceeds the emf.
Think about the current if there were no series resistor.

levels.title: Cells in series
levels.adds: New idea: series emfs add or subtract depending on the way round, and resistances add (Section 3.11).
hints: If the cells help each other, add the emfs. If they oppose, subtract.
The current passes through both cells, so their internal resistances add.
The equivalent emf stays positive: the larger cell wins.

levels.title: Cells in parallel
levels.adds: More steps: ε = (ε₁r₂ + ε₂r₁)/(r₁ + r₂) and 1/r = 1/r₁ + 1/r₂, then I = ε/(R + r) (Section 3.11).
hints: The equivalent emf lies between the two emfs.
The cell with the smaller internal resistance counts for more.
Treat the pair as one cell and find the current in the resistor.

misconceptions: The terminal voltage of a cell equals its emf
The terminal voltage is the same while charging as while discharging
Cells in series always add their emfs
Two cells in parallel give twice the emf
